questions.prompt: OAuth 2.0 already gives your app an access token. What does OpenID Connect add on top of it?
options: Identity: an `id_token` that tells your app who the user is
Authorization: permission to call the user's APIs
A way to skip the consent screen entirely
Encryption of the access token so the client can read it
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 gives authorization but deliberately says nothing about identity. OIDC adds that: include `openid` in the scope and the token response also carries an `id_token`.

questions.prompt: Put the "Sign in with Google" OIDC interaction in order.
steps: The website redirects the browser to Google with an OIDC request for the user's basic profile
Google asks the user to log in and to consent to sharing their details
Google redirects back and provides an access token and an ID token
The website verifies Google's signature on the ID token and logs the user in
questions.explanation: The four stages are the request, the authentication, the token exchange and the verification of the signed ID token.

questions.prompt: Which `id_token` claim should you persist as the user's permanent identifier at the provider?
options: `email`, because every user has exactly one
`sub`, because it is unique and never changes
`iat`, because it records when the user signed up
questions.explanation: `sub` is the user's permanent, unique ID at the provider. The lesson warns never to use email as a primary key, because users can change their email.

questions.prompt: What is the Discovery endpoint (`/.well-known/openid-configuration`) for?
options: Fetching extra user claims with the access token
A machine-readable JSON document listing the provider's endpoints, scopes, signing algorithms and JWKS URI
Exchanging the authorization code for tokens
Registering your app to receive a `client_id` and `client_secret`
questions.explanation: Your .NET middleware fetches the discovery document once on startup and configures itself from it. Fetching extra claims is the UserInfo endpoint's job.

questions.prompt: Why does Google's token endpoint require both the `code` and the `client_secret`?
options: The `code` proves a specific user just consented, and the `client_secret` proves the request really comes from your app
The `client_secret` identifies the user, and the `code` identifies the app
Either one is enough; sending both only makes the request faster
The `code` is reused for every login, so the `client_secret` makes it unique
questions.explanation: A code alone could be stolen from the front channel, and a secret alone says nothing about a user consenting right now. Both checks must pass.

source.section: How they're related — why BOTH are required together
